## Today's Agenda

- The two layers of meaning in a message
- Sorting your own notes into easy and hard
- Sampling what you observe
- Edge cases, and the rules they become

## Four Corrections From Your Topics

- **Both rounds of this study are content analysis**
    - You build a codebook, then you apply it
    - No surveys, no interviews, no focus groups
- **If your unit is a person, the question needs rewriting**
    - You cannot ask them anything
    - Move the unit from the person to the message
- **Three questions is a ceiling, not a target**
    - Eight questions means none has been chosen yet
- **One coder means stability, not agreement**
    - You re-code your own work after 48 hours

Six of you proposed a method this course does not run. That is fixable this week.

## Which Scale Is Yours

- **The model prospectus is written at professional scale**
    - 1,500 messages, which is what a publishable study costs
    - That is the example, not the assignment
- **Your scale is set by your budget**
    - Two to four hours, so 250 items at 45 seconds
    - Fifty coded units is the floor
- **Nobody lost a point on this**
    - Size is graded on the Sampling Plan in November, with arithmetic

Same mechanics either way. If you wrote 1,500, keep the design and resize it.

## Numbers You Look Up

- **Retrieved counts are welcome**
    - Box office, Rotten Tomatoes, view counts, stream counts
- **They cannot be the whole study**
    - Something in it has to be coded by you
- **Pair them**
    - Code the thumbnails, compare to the view counts
    - Code the reviews, compare to the box office

A study made only of numbers you looked up gives the codebook nothing to do.

## The Argument You Will Have

- **You will disagree with yourself**
    - Same chat message, two readings, a week apart
    - Neither reading is wrong, exactly
- **Today is about seeing it coming**
    - Build the codebook that settles it in advance
    - Not at eleven at night in November

You leave having sorted your field notes into the easy half and the hard half.

## Two Layers in Every Message

[Krippendorff, 2018]{.eyebrow}

- **Manifest content:** what is explicitly on the surface
    - Countable almost mechanically, given one clear rule
- **Latent content:** the underlying meaning
    - It takes interpretation to reach

The split sits at the center of codebook design, and most first codebooks treat a latent
variable as manifest.

## Manifest Content

Features any trained coder can identify with high agreement:

- Does the message contain an `@` mention?
- Is it shorter than ten characters?
- Does it contain a known emote token?
- How many words is it?

These are countable almost mechanically, and the work is writing one clear rule.

## Latent Content

Features you cannot read off the surface:

- Is the message friendly or hostile?
- Is it directed at the streamer, or performing for the room?
- Is "first" a genuine claim or a running joke?
- Is the mood of chat celebratory or restless?

**Two careful coders can disagree about every one of these in good faith.**

## The Argument for Watching

- **Latent coding needs an interpretive framework**
    - It turns an impression into a defensible judgment
    - That framework gets built by watching
- **Twenty hours of live Twitch teaches the pattern**
    - A wall of one emote after a big play is celebration
    - Learned by watching it happen, repeatedly
- Immersion is how latent content becomes codeable

## Your Turn {.discuss}

- From your field notes, name one clearly **manifest** thing
- Name one clearly **latent**, and how you might code it two ways
- What surface feature could stand as evidence for the latent one?

## Sorting Your Notes

- **Mark every observation M or L**
    - Manifest items are variables you could write today
    - Latent items will need **decision rules**
- **A workable codebook mixes both**
    - Two or three manifest measures, one that takes judgment
- All latent, and your reliability check is going to hurt

## Sampling Your Observation

- **You cannot watch all of it, and need not**
- **What you need is a structured sample**
    - It should reflect the range of the thing you study
- **Ten large competitive-gaming channels teach you one thing**
    - About everything else they will actively mislead you

## Match Your Source's Range

- **The class dataset spans a deliberate range**
    - 50 channels across the volume distribution
    - Gaming and non-gaming, crowded and nearly empty
- **That range is the principle, not the assignment**
    - Span whatever source you settled on with the librarian
- **On Twitch:** big channels and small, gaming and art
- **On a subreddit:** busy threads and dead ones
- **On a news site:** the front page and the unlinked pages
- **Sample across time as well**
    - A feed at peak and in a quiet hour are different rooms

## Coverage Beats Volume

- **Twenty streams spanning the variety beat fifty alike**
- **The same principle keeps returning**
    - The wide literature search sees the whole conversation
    - Statistical sampling later in the term does the same
- Representativeness is a discipline at every stage

## When Channels Are Live

[Figure 7.1, the collection week]{.eyebrow}

- **Eight channels across the distribution**, November 18 to 24
- **Large channels are live daily**, for long stretches
- **Small channels appear once or twice all week**
    - A random two-hour window catches the big ones easily
    - It catches the small ones only if you place it
- Scheduling your observation is a sampling decision

## The Edge-Case Log

Some of what you observe resists every category you are tempted to draw. Those moments are
the single most useful thing observation produces.

Keep an **edge-case log** beside your field notes. For each case: log it, say what makes it
ambiguous, and list the ways a codebook could handle it.

## Four Edge Cases

- **A message of pure emotes**, no words
    - Directed, broadcast, or a different object entirely?
- **Copypasta:** a block every regular pastes unread
    - A message, and not written by that viewer in any normal sense
- **A language you do not read**
- **An obvious bot**, or a joke wearing the streamer's name

## Edge Cases Become Rules

- **These are the raw material of decision rules**
    - The model prospectus carried "unclassifiable"
    - The log is how you learn what lands in it
- **A codebook without one pays later**
    - It meets these messages first during coding
    - A codebook with one has already decided

## Knowing When to Stop

Four signs immersion has done its job:

- New streams stop surprising you
- You can name three to five dimensions that matter
- The edge-case log has enough entries to write rules
- Your notes repeat themselves rather than adding

This is **saturation** again, the same idea the literature search used.

## What You Walk Away With

- **Conceptual clarity** about your variables in this medium
- **Candidate categories** for each one
- The beginnings of the **decision rules** for hard cases
- Enough context to spot a surface feature about to mislead

Those four are the raw material of a codebook, which is what you build next.

- **Finish your notes and edge-case log**
    - Three or more sessions, big and small, gaming and not
    - Mark each entry manifest or latent

- **Write two or three candidate questions**

## Due Friday: The Prospectus

- **One page, 250 to 400 words, six headed sections**
    - Descriptive title, questions, theoretical framework
    - The gap, method overview, expected contribution
    - Plus a rough timeline by assignment
- **The method overview names how much data**
    - Budget two to four hours of coding
    - 250 chat messages at 45 seconds is about three hours
    - Fifty coded units is the floor
- **Going over one page is a diagnostic, not a formatting error**
